**Why Tides Happen**

Tides are one of nature’s most fascinating and rhythmic phenomena, shaping coastlines and influencing marine life in predictable yet powerful ways. At their core, tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth’s oceans. The Moon, being much closer to our planet than the Sun, exerts the strongest force, pulling the water toward it and creating a bulge, or high tide, on the side of Earth facing the Moon. But you might wonder why there’s also a high tide on the opposite side of the planet. This happens because the Moon’s gravity doesn’t just pull the water—it also affects Earth itself. The gravitational force causes Earth’s crust to shift slightly, and the centrifugal force from this movement creates another bulge in the oceans on the far side. These two bulges result in the regular rise and fall of sea levels we experience as tides.

The Sun plays a role too, though its influence is weaker because it’s so much farther away. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth align during a full or new moon, their gravitational forces combine, producing spring tides—higher high tides and lower low tides. Conversely, when they form a right angle during a quarter moon, their effects partially cancel each other out, leading to neap tides, which are less extreme.

Earth’s rotation also contributes to the timing of tides. As our planet spins, different areas move into and out of these bulges, experiencing two high tides and two low tides roughly every 24 hours and 50 minutes. This is because the Moon’s position shifts slightly as Earth rotates, and the tidal cycle follows the lunar day, which is longer than a solar day.

The shape of coastlines, the depth of the ocean, and other geographical factors can amplify or diminish tides. In some places, like the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the coastline funnels the tidal bulge into an extremely high tide, while in others, tides may be barely noticeable.
